Meta Platforms shares break out, signaling renewed market momentum
A 36% monthly surge powered by the Muse AI agent has Meta knocking on the door of $2 trillion in market cap.
Meta Platforms just posted its best month in over a decade, and the catalyst wasn’t a metaverse pivot or another Instagram feature. It was an AI agent called Muse.
Shares of Meta climbed roughly 36% through September 24, 2026, marking the stock’s strongest monthly performance since July 2013. The stock hit $777.59, pushing Meta’s market capitalization to approximately $1.98 trillion.
The inflection point arrived on September 8, when Meta launched Muse, a personal AI agent that quickly became the number one app on the Apple App Store.
On September 21 alone, Meta shares surged 11.34% in a single session.
Analysts are projecting that Muse could eventually generate up to $50 billion in annual revenue, with costs that remain manageable relative to that upside. The monetization playbook reportedly includes a freemium model alongside enhanced advertising capabilities. Wall Street responded accordingly, with multiple analysts raising their price targets for Meta into a range between $860 and $995.

Through mid-August 2026, Meta shares were down approximately 18% year-to-date, with investors uneasy about the company’s massive capital expenditure on AI infrastructure. A legal settlement also helped clear the air during this period, removing an overhang that had weighed on sentiment.
Meta’s success with Muse validates a thesis that consumer AI applications can achieve immediate, massive adoption when built on top of an existing user base. Meta already had the audience and built the AI tool to serve them, resulting in an app store chart-topper within days of launch.
The projected $50 billion revenue ceiling analysts have floated for Muse, if it materializes even partially, would represent a meaningful new business line for Meta. For context, Meta’s trailing advertising revenue stood at approximately $228 billion.
Upcoming earnings reports will be the next major test, with investors expecting early monetization metrics for Muse, retention data beyond the initial download spike, and guidance on expanding the agent’s capabilities. Meta’s annual Connect developer event is also being closely watched for further strategic developments heading into the fourth quarter of 2026.

Mark Cuban says Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads as Meta docs reveal $16 billion in fraud-linked revenue
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 2:30 PM PDT 5 min read
Andrew Harnik/Getty Images/Finn Gomez/Getty Images
Mark Cuban keeps getting emails about a $294 diabetes cure he has never sold.
"Every single week I get emails from little old men and ladies saying, 'Will my cure for diabetes work?' or 'I just ordered your cure for diabetes for $294,'" the 68-year-old billionaire investor said on an August episode of Pivot, the podcast hosted by Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway.

Those ads are deepfakes built with an AI copy of his face and voice, Cuban said, and Meta (NASDAQ:META) runs them anyway. "Facebook knows the little old ladies are getting ripped off," he said. He called the platform "the worst of the worst."
Cuban said some of the ads even include a disclaimer admitting the person on screen is AI-generated and the clip is meant as entertainment. By the time anyone gets to it, he argued, the pitch has already worked. "And to Facebook, that's good enough," he said.
"The point is, that defines the culture of the organization," Cuban said. A company that lets scammers go after people's grandparents, he argued, has shown what it will tolerate at every level.
Cuban does run a drug company — he co-founded Cost Plus Drugs, an online pharmacy that sells low-cost generic medications.
On Nov. 6, 2025, Reuters reported on internal Meta documents showing the company expected roughly $16 billion, or about 10% of its 2024 revenue, to flow in from ads pushing scams and prohibited products. By Meta's own internal count, users across its apps were seeing some 15 billion "higher risk" ads a day — the ones with obvious markers of fraud. One late 2024 document put that category's value at about $7 billion a year.
In a May 2025 presentation, Meta's own safety staff estimated the company's platforms play a part in a third of the scams that succeed in the U.S. Before Meta bans an advertiser, its automated systems must peg the account as at least 95% likely to be running a scam, the documents say. Below that threshold, the suspected scammer simply pays more per ad and stays live.
Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Reuters the documents "present a selective view that distorts Meta's approach to fraud and scams," and called the company's 10% estimate "rough and overly-inclusive." Complaints from users about scam ads had fallen 58% over the prior 18 months, he said at the time, and the company pulled down more than 134 million scam ads in 2025. The same documents note the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Meta over advertising tied to financial fraud.
Meanwhile, Meta's newest AI product has been causing headaches of its own. A Toronto man let the company's AI agent run his Facebook Marketplace listings on Sept. 26, and it gave a buyer his street address and said yes to a lowball offer. He later traced part of the problem to a permission setting he'd picked.
Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors
Older Americans lose more to this kind of crime than any other age group. People 60 and older told the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center they lost $7.7 billion in 2025, across 201,266 complaints — 59% more money than the year before, according to the bureau's 2025 Internet Crime Report. Investment schemes did the worst damage at $3.5 billion, with tech and customer support scams taking another $1.04 billion.
AI showed up in more than 3,100 of those complaints, and together those victims lost over $352 million. That's only counting the people who spoke up — plenty never file at all.
How to protect yourself — and your parents
Anytime you see a famous face advertising something pop up in your feed, assume it's fake — Cuban himself included in that. Run the product's name through a search with the word "scam" next to it. Then think about who in your family is on Facebook the most – and send them a message warning them about it.
And if you suspect anything fishy, file a report the same day to the Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov. The FBI froze $32.9 million worth of funds tied to older victims' cases in 2025, the agency says, but it can only chase money it knows about.
Moneywise reached out to Meta for comment on Cuban's reply but did not immediately receive a response.

XLK Does Not Own Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Netflix or Tesla. Three Stocks Are 35.87% of It
Millions of investors bought XLK expecting broad exposure to the companies reshaping the economy, but a closer look at its SEC filing reveals several of the most recognizable names in tech are nowhere inside it, and the ones that are…
Published October 6, 2026, 6:33pm ET · 4 min read
The ETF Examiner desk. Editor: Ryne Mauck.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A couple intently reviews financial data on their laptop, reflecting the serious consideration investors give to their portfolios, especially when dealing with specific ETFs like XLK. © 24/7 Wall St.
If you bought a popular tech sector ETF for broad technology exposure, open its most recent SEC portfolio filing. As of June 30, 2026, the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLK) held no shares of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Netflix, or Tesla. In the same filing, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction), Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) made up 35.87% of the fund. The ten largest positions came to 64.45%.
That gap between what’s missing and what dominates is the fund’s main limitation for investors seeking broad tech exposure. The word “technology” on the label covers a much narrower and more concentrated piece of the market than most buyers expect.
What Your Technology Fund Actually Holds
The filing lists 74 equity positions supporting about $123.9 billion in net assets. NVIDIA led at 14.65%, Apple came next at 12.85%, and Microsoft held 8.38%. Three more chip companies each had more than 5%, and chip equipment suppliers took up most of the other top-ten spots. At the other end, dozens of positions each made up less than 0.5% of assets.
So investors expecting broad exposure to the tech economy own a portfolio driven by a small group of semiconductor and hardware companies.
Why Alphabet and Amazon Fall Outside the Fund
XLK tracks a sector index built on the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS). GICS assigns every public company to exactly one sector. It puts Alphabet, Meta, and Netflix in Communication Services and Amazon and Tesla in Consumer Discretionary. XLK only holds companies classified as Information Technology.
GICS sorts companies by how they make money. Alphabet and Meta earn most of their revenue from advertising. Amazon’s classification follows its retail operations, and Tesla’s follows its vehicle manufacturing business. That means a highly technological business can still end up in a different sector.
All of this is disclosed and standard practice. The classification is public, and the fund follows its index. The cost comes from a common habit: few buyers read the sector definition before they buy a sector fund.
Concentration Risk Behind a Sector Label
When several of the biggest tech-adjacent companies are left out, the giants that remain carry more weight. With 74 stocks and 35.87% of assets in just three of them, XLK’s results depend heavily on NVIDIA, Apple, and Microsoft. A prolonged decline in any one of them could move the whole fund more than its name suggests.
That concentration has paid off recently. XLK gained 41.07% over the year ending October 5, 2026. Concentration amplifies losses as well as gains, and a retiree who draws income from a portfolio feels the losses more. Investors who want AI exposure without piling further into the same three chip and hardware names have options beyond the semiconductor sector (we covered seven of them, from power to cooling to networking, in a free report you can grab here).
XLK won’t give you either Alphabet or Amazon. Adding an S&P 500 fund changes the math in a way many investors miss. The broad fund already owns those companies at market weight, so XLK on top mostly adds more NVIDIA, Apple, and Microsoft to a portfolio that already holds them.
It works the other way too. If you already own large stakes in any of those three companies directly, buying XLK could double your exposure.
A Broader Tech ETF Includes Alphabet and Meta
The iShares U.S. Technology ETF (NYSEARCA:IYW) tracks the Russell 1000 Technology RIC 22.5/45 Capped Index, which classifies companies differently. Its top holdings have included Alphabet and Meta Platforms. The Vanguard Information Technology ETF follows a GICS-based index. It leaves out the same companies XLK does. Check each issuer’s current factsheet for expense ratios and top-ten weights before you compare.
XLK suits investors wanting concentrated exposure to the GICS Information Technology sector (chips, hardware, and enterprise software) and comfortable with a top-heavy portfolio. XLK is the wrong product for investors seeking broad technology exposure that includes the platforms most people call Big Tech.
Keep the dates in mind. These holdings come from the June 30, 2026 SEC filing. Weights change, and index providers review classifications from time to time, so a company can be moved to a different sector. Before you buy any sector fund, read the index methodology that defines the sector. That document tells you what you actually own.

News of Meta Platforms (META -0.41%) launching a personal artificial intelligence (AI) agent called Muse last month gave the struggling stock some much-needed life. It's now in positive territory for the year, up around 12% since January. It's been a tremendous turnaround story for the company, as it's made investors believers of Meta's AI strategy.
But I don't think it'll last. While the launch of a personal AI assistant may unlock new opportunities and drive more growth, since there are paid plans as well, here's why I don't think it'll be successful.
Image source: Getty Images.
AI agents need to be trusted, and that's not Meta's strength
AI agents could potentially add a lot of efficiency to someone's life. They could respond to emails, book dinners, make travel plans, and even shop online for them. But each one of those examples also requires the user to allow the agent to act on their behalf, and thus, to trust it to make sound decisions. It may also involve allowing them to access sensitive information.
Meta, unfortunately, doesn't have the best track record for protecting user privacy. It's faced numerous privacy-related lawsuits and recently agreed to pay $18 billion to settle lawsuits that alleged its social media apps harmed children.
Given that there is a growing amount of competition in AI and there will be many AI agents available, I'm skeptical about just how much people will be willing to trust a service from Meta, given its track record. As concerns grow about the level of access that an AI can have, I think users will be less inclined to use an AI from a company such as Meta. While its AI agent may provide convenience for users who heavily use the company's social media apps, I don't think it'll be a big growth driver for the business.

Meta's stock has been volatile over the past year, as even with its recent surge in value, it's still only up around 3% in the last 12 months. It's trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 28, which is a fair bit higher than the S&P 500 average of 23. The tech stock is by no means a steal of a deal.
Plus, when factoring in the risks of its AI strategy not paying off plus the money pit that is its metaverse segment, it quickly becomes apparent why the stock should arguably trade at a discount rather than a premium. This is a stock that could be vulnerable to a sizable decline if there's a downturn in the markets.

Meta Platforms (META) Stock Drops 3% Amid AI Sector Turbulence
By Trader EdgeSeptember 28, 2026No Comments4 Mins Read
Meta Platforms shares declined during Monday’s premarket session, potentially marking consecutive down days for the first time since August’s midpoint.
Despite a 3% Friday retreat and Monday’s early weakness, September gains still total an impressive 32%.
The decline coincides with broader artificial intelligence sector weakness following OpenAI’s decision to halt training on new models.
Wall Street maintains a predominantly positive stance, with analyst targets spanning $855 to $950 driven by Muse’s promising start.
Jefferies highlights Muse’s expanding use cases, describing the AI assistant as an unexpectedly successful product launch.
Meta stock experienced another downturn Monday, retreating approximately 3% before the opening bell. This movement followed Friday’s similar 3% decline, threatening to deliver consecutive negative sessions for the first time since August’s middle stretch.
Despite this recent weakness, September has delivered exceptional returns for Meta shareholders. Through Friday’s closing bell, the stock had surged 32% during the month.
The bulk of this impressive run connects directly to Muse, the company’s standalone AI personal assistant. Following its September 8 debut, the application rapidly ascended to dominant positions across major app distribution platforms.
However, the momentum from that launch appears to be cooling. This development leaves investors questioning the stock’s trajectory moving forward.
Some of the selling pressure originates from factors beyond Meta‘s direct control. OpenAI recently announced a temporary halt to training activities on its most recent model iterations, citing the need to implement enhanced safety protocols before proceeding.
This development has created headwinds across AI-focused equities, with Meta caught in the broader downdraft. According to BNP Paribas analyst Nick Jones, the critical narrative for shareholders has shifted toward competitive dynamics.
“Moving forward, we think investors should monitor expected rollouts of rival consumer AI assistants, especially from major platforms including Google and OpenAI,” Jones stated in his Friday evening research note.
Despite these concerns, Jones maintains a constructive view with an $855 target, suggesting 14% potential appreciation from Friday’s closing level.
Muse generates income primarily through modest transaction-based charges. Jones emphasizes that the application’s long-term revenue model remains unclear for the investment community.
He identifies advertising as a plausible future revenue stream, despite Meta’s current strategy of keeping Muse advertisement-free.

Meta’s shares last traded at $751.66, sitting just 1% beneath the 52-week peak of $779.82.

The firm expressed surprise at the complexity of tasks users have delegated to Muse within weeks of launch, including parking violation payments and elaborate tracking system construction.

Meta Platforms (META) Stock Jumps 27% After Muse Download Surge and Legal Settlement
Meta (META) stock jumped 27% in a month as its Muse AI agent surges past 5 million downloads and legal settlements ease pressure.
By Trader EdgeOctober 2, 20264 Mins Read
Meta’s stock has climbed 27% over the past four weeks, though it’s still down about 1% over the past 12 months.
The company’s new AI agent, Muse, has topped iOS download charts and reportedly passed 5 million downloads.
Meta launched a new Meta Enterprise Platform to sell AI tools to other businesses.
Meta settled many state lawsuits over alleged harm to young users, agreeing to pay up to $18 billion over a decade.
QRG Capital Management increased its Meta stake by 5.5% in the second quarter, and Wall Street holds a “Moderate Buy” rating with a $787.86 average price target.
Meta Platforms (META) stock closed at $725.93 on Friday, up 0.1% on the day. The stock has gained 27% over the past month, a sharp turnaround after a rough stretch.
Over the past 12 months, META is still down roughly 1%. But recent momentum suggests the tide may be turning.
Much of the renewed interest centers on Muse, Meta’s personalized AI agent released on September 8. It quickly became one of the most downloaded apps in the U.S.
Reports now say Muse has surpassed 5 million downloads. JPMorgan analysts noted the free-access approach could pressure subscription rivals while opening new advertising and commerce opportunities.
Muse is free up to a point, with a paid tier for extra features. But the bigger opportunity may be commerce.
Meta has said it plans to charge merchants when Muse helps users complete purchases. That could turn a popular app into a real revenue engine, assuming adoption keeps growing.
The company is also expanding Muse for small businesses, tying AI tools directly to advertising and sales. That’s a logical next step for a company that still earns most of its money from ads.
Competition is heating up fast, though. OpenAI launched its own personal AI agent, Dots, and Google and Apple are reportedly working on similar products too.
Meta also announced a new venture on September 28 called Meta Enterprise Platform. It will sell AI tools and software to other companies, built on the same infrastructure Meta has used internally.
The company already has deep relationships with businesses through its advertising ecosystem. That could give it a head start over newer entrants.
Meta has also cleared up a chunk of its legal overhang. The company settled many lawsuits brought by a bipartisan group of state attorneys general over alleged harm to young users.
Meta agreed to pay up to approximately $18 billion over a decade, with part of that contingent on actions by YouTube and TikTok. It will also add new protections for teens on its apps.
More lawsuits remain, but resolving this major group of claims removes a source of uncertainty that weighed on the stock.
On the institutional side, QRG Capital Management increased its Meta position by 5.5% in the second quarter. The fund now holds 372,579 shares worth about $209.9 million.
Other funds made smaller moves too. Advantage Trust Co, Philadelphia Investment Partners, and Axiom Investment Management all opened new positions during the quarter.
Analysts remain largely positive. Meta carries a “Moderate Buy” consensus rating with an average price target of $787.86, even as some firms have trimmed their targets.
Not everything is rosy. Meta’s AI spending is expected to top $130 billion, and free cash flow has declined as a result.
Insider selling has also drawn attention. COO Javier Olivan and board member Christopher Cox both sold shares in late September under pre-arranged trading plans.
Meta last reported earnings on July 29, posting $6.18 EPS against estimates of $7.19. Revenue came in at $60.80 billion, above the $60.22 billion analysts expected, with quarterly revenue up 28% year over year.

Nebius Group signs $27B AI capacity deal with Meta Platforms
The five-year agreement dwarfs a prior $3 billion contract between the two companies and positions Nebius as a major force in AI infrastructure beyond the hyperscaler giants.
Nebius Group just locked in one of the largest AI infrastructure contracts on record. The Netherlands-based company signed a five-year deal with Meta Platforms worth up to approximately $27 billion, a figure that would make it one of the most significant commitments a non-hyperscaler has ever secured from a Big Tech partner.
The deal includes $12 billion in dedicated GPU capacity and up to $15 billion in additional AI capacity purchases, contingent on that capacity remaining unsold to other customers.
The $12 billion dedicated portion of the contract will deploy Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform, the next-generation GPU architecture that’s becoming the backbone of frontier AI training workloads. Deployments are expected to begin in early 2027 across Nebius data center locations in Finland, the UK, and the US.
The remaining $15 billion functions as a backstop mechanism. If Nebius can’t sell certain capacity to third-party customers, Meta steps in to absorb it. For Nebius, this essentially creates a revenue floor. For Meta, it guarantees access to compute resources without the capital expenditure headache of building every rack itself.
To put the scale in perspective, Nebius signed a $3 billion contract with Meta just four months prior, in November 2025. Going from $3 billion to $27 billion is a ninefold increase in commitment.

Nebius originally spun out of Yandex, the Russian tech conglomerate, after restructuring in 2024. Unity Software (NYSE:U | U Price Prediction) stock rose 5% to $41.56 as traders weighed the company’s newly announced day-one support for Meta VR Glasses. The product news arrives as Unity works to reinforce its role in extended-reality development, though concerns around sales growth and billings still give investors reasons to remain selective.
The broader software group also moved higher. The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (BATS:IGV) gained 1.5% to $106.81, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE ARCA:SPY) added 0.41% to $767.30.
Unity announced immediate engine support for Meta VR Glasses, Meta Platforms’ next-generation virtual-reality device that is expected to reach retail customers in spring 2027. Unity said developers can begin building and testing experiences now, providing more time to prepare titles for the device’s launch.
For existing Quest developers, Unity said projects built with OpenXR can carry forward with minimal changes. The company also highlighted support for eye and hand tracking, quad views rendering that can reduce GPU demands, and spatial-audio tools designed for more immersive experiences.
Unity’s early compatibility could make the engine more attractive to studios planning games, entertainment products, training software, and other immersive applications for Meta VR Glasses. The company said developers can test certain VR Glasses interactions within the Unity Editor before receiving physical hardware.
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) is central to the opportunity because Meta VR Glasses will sit within the same ecosystem as Meta’s existing Quest products. Unity said existing Quest apps can run on VR Glasses from day one, which could reduce development friction for studios already using Unity’s tools.
That compatibility matters because developers typically prefer to reuse assets, workflows, and code across multiple devices when possible. Unity’s product announcement emphasized a single codebase that can support multiple platforms, potentially helping studios reach additional players without rebuilding projects from scratch.
The opportunity, however, depends on adoption after Meta brings VR Glasses to market. Unity may need to demonstrate that developers are using the new tools, launching successful projects, and expanding their subscriptions or platform spending before the announcement becomes a meaningful financial catalyst.
Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) stock climbed 3% to $239.37, adding to the software-sector strength. Adobe remains closely associated with creative and document software, making Adobe stock a familiar way for investors to track demand for productivity tools and AI-enhanced workflows.
Intuit (NASDAQ:INTU) stock gained 2% to $273.21 as software names broadly advanced. Intuit operates consumer and business-focused financial software platforms, and Intuit stock can respond to expectations for customer growth, recurring revenue, and operating leverage.
The gains in Adobe stock and Intuit stock helped show that Unity’s move was not occurring in complete isolation. Still, Unity’s 5% rise outpaced both peers and the IGV ETF, suggesting that the Meta VR Glasses news gave traders a company-specific reason to focus on Unity.
Unity Stock: Growth Questions Remain Important
The positive product headline does not eliminate the concerns surrounding Unity’s underlying business performance. Recent commentary has pointed to stagnant sales, slower billings growth, and a stock that has remained under pressure despite the latest 5% advance.
Unity’s long-term case may depend on whether new platform support translates into broader Create-segment demand and more durable revenue growth. The company has a clear technical story around VR Glasses, yet investors will likely want evidence that product momentum is producing measurable business results.
For now, Unity stock has a timely catalyst, while Adobe stock and Intuit stock are participating in a broader software-sector rally. Investors should watch for signs that Unity’s VR Glasses support leads to new developer adoption, launch titles, and stronger financial metrics, while keeping position sizes modest given the company’s execution risks.

The digital advertising landscape is shifting as artificial intelligence transforms how users find information and connect online. Choosing between Alphabet (GOOGL +0.35%) (GOOG +0.22%) and Meta Platforms (META -0.41%) requires weighing search dominance against social media scale.
Alphabet remains the primary gateway to the internet through its Google search engine and YouTube, while Meta dominates the social landscape with its massive family of apps. Both companies rely heavily on advertising revenue, but their paths to growth in artificial intelligence and the future of hardware are beginning to diverge significantly for investors of the communication sector.
Alphabet operates as a diversified technology holding company, primarily selling digital advertising space through its dominant Search platform and YouTube. It also provides cloud computing services to businesses and develops the Android operating system to support its mobile ecosystem.
In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $402.8 billion, representing a year-over-year growth of 15.1%. This expansion helped drive a net income of $132.2 billion, which was significantly higher than the profit recorded in the previous year. The net margin, which measures how much of each dollar in sales is kept as profit after all expenses, improved to 32.8% compared to the prior period.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.1x, indicating that total debt is very low relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at 2.0x, which means the company has twice as many short-term assets as short-term liabilities to cover its bills. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was $73.3 billion, which is the cash generated after paying for operations and capital expenditures.
Meta Platforms builds technologies for human connection through its family of apps, including Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. The company primarily generates revenue by selling highly targeted advertising space to marketers and creators who want to reach its billions of global users. It also offers consumer hardware products through its Reality Labs division, where it maintains complex relationships with mobile operating system providers such as Apple (AAPL +0.22%) and Google that influence its advertising effectiveness.
In FY 2025, revenue reached $201.0 billion, which indicates a robust growth rate of 22.2% from the prior year. Despite this revenue growth, net income was $60.5 billion, which was slightly lower than the profit recorded in the previous year. The net margin for the company was 30.1%, showing it remains highly profitable even as it spends on new initiatives, such as AI data centers.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.4x, suggesting a conservative amount of debt compared to its equity. The current ratio is 2.6x, providing a healthy cushion for the company to meet its immediate financial obligations with its existing assets. Free cash flow for the year was $46.1 billion.
Alphabet faces significant regulatory challenges, including a final judgment in a Department of Justice case that may require sharing search data or structural changes. The business is also sensitive to economic downturns that could reduce advertising spending across its Google search and YouTube platforms. Furthermore, the company must manage high capital costs for artificial intelligence infrastructure while facing competition from rivals such as Microsoft.
Meta recently settled a multistate lawsuit for $17.1 billion, which requires the company to implement sweeping child-safety reforms on its social platforms. It also faces ongoing risks from changes in mobile operating systems made by partners like Apple, which can limit the effectiveness of its advertising tools. Additionally, the Reality Labs segment continues to report persistent operating losses as the company tries to develop its long-term hardware and metaverse strategy.
While Meta Platforms offers higher top-line growth, Alphabet trades at a higher valuation multiple based on future earnings estimates and sales. The Forward P/E ratio compares a company's stock price to its future earnings estimates, while the P/S ratio measures market cap relative to sales over the past twelve months.
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Alphabet and Meta depend on digital advertising to support their businesses, yet both are looking to artificial intelligence to fuel success in future years. Alphabet is spending so much on building out its AI infrastructure, it reported negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion in the second quarter of 2026, as capital expenditures nearly doubled year over year to $44.9 billion.
Meta has fared better despite also nearly doubling capex, as its Q2 free cash flow totaled $784 million. However, that was a steep decline from 2025's free cash flow of $8.5 billion.
Yet that spending may be worth it. Meta's recent release of its Muse AI assistant achieved five million downloads in 22 days, more than popular AI tools such as ChatGPT. Even so, I would invest in Alphabet rather than Meta.
That's because Alphabet has so many ways in which it can employ AI to deliver business growth. Its Waymo autonomous ride-hailing business relies on AI as the driver for its vehicles. The company's cloud computing division, Google Cloud, through which it delivers its proprietary AI models to customers for a fee, experienced 82% year-over-year sales growth to $24.8 billion. This rapid rise in revenue indicates clients are adopting Alphabet's AI offerings, suggesting its capex spending can pay off in the long run.

Meta Platforms stock (ISIN US30303M1027) last closed at USD 648.03 on Nasdaq on September 11, 2026, leaving the company valued at about USD 1.65 trillion and giving investors a visible AI-driven rerating story around its new Muse agent and ongoing legal settlement effects.
Muse AI and settlement sharpen the growth story
According to Investing.com on September 14, 2026, Goldman Sachs reiterated its Buy rating on Meta Platforms and kept a 12-month price target of USD 725, stating that it views the stock with increased conviction after Meta agreed to settle litigation over its services for minors and launched its new Muse AI agent.
As Sina Finance reported on September 14, 2026, Goldman Sachs highlighted Muse AI as a shift from simple chatbots toward intelligent agents that can autonomously execute real-world tasks, and it calculated that the USD 725 target implies 11.9% upside from the reference price of USD 648.03.
For investors, the key takeaway is that the combination of a resolved legal overhang and a new class of AI products has turned Muse into a central medium-term catalyst, even as some analysts still express caution about the timing of monetization.
Q2 2026 earnings show strong revenue, weaker margins
Meta Platforms has already reported results for the second quarter of its fiscal year ending December 2026, covering the period from April to June 2026.
According to an earnings analysis from Rakuten Securities on September 14, 2026, Meta generated revenue of USD 60.801 billion in Q2 2026, an increase of 28.0% compared with the same quarter of the prior year.
The same report from Rakuten Securities noted that operating income in Q2 2026 reached USD 18.775 billion, which represented an 8.2% decline year on year as sharply higher research and development spending and roughly USD 2.4 billion in litigation-related costs weighed on profitability.
Looking at the core advertising business, Rakuten Securities reported that advertising revenue rose 27.5% year on year to USD 59.363 billion in Q2 2026, while the Family of Apps segment delivered USD 60.370 billion in revenue and USD 23.394 billion in operating profit, the latter falling 6.3% from the prior-year quarter.
The same analysis also pointed out that Meta guided for Q3 2026 revenue in a range of USD 61 billion to USD 64 billion, which corresponds to year-on-year growth between 19.0% and 24.9%, but it cautioned that new restrictions on social media use by minors in the United States could start to weigh on advertising growth from Q3 onward.
Consensus points to double-digit upside despite skepticism on Muse
Wall Street remains broadly positive on Meta Platforms despite debate about how quickly Muse and other AI agents will translate into revenue.
According to MarketBeat as of September 13, 2026, Meta Platforms carries a consensus rating of Moderate Buy based on 4 Strong Buy ratings, 34 Buy ratings and 9 Hold ratings, and it has an average analyst price target of USD 787.54, implying around 21.5% upside from the closing price of USD 648.03.
The same overview from MarketBeat shows a 52-week trading range between USD 520.26 and USD 790.80 for Meta stock, which situates the recent price roughly in the middle of that band and still about 18.1% below the 52-week high.
As StockAnalysis reported on September 13, 2026, a separate compilation of Wall Street estimates points to an average price target of USD 754.15, about 16.4% above the same USD 648.03 reference price, and classifies the stock with a Strong Buy consensus based on 62 analyst opinions.
For investors, the quantified gap between the current share price and the analyst target range in the mid-700s to low-800s underscores that the Street is still assigning significant value to Meta's AI roadmap, even if individual houses differ in how aggressively they factor Muse and other agentic products into their models.
Analyst actions around Muse highlight both optimism and risk
Recent individual analyst calls around Muse illustrate the spectrum from enthusiasm to caution.
As Blockonomi reported on September 14, 2026, Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian maintained a Hold rating on Meta but raised his price target by 9% from USD 595 to USD 650 on September 11, 2026, leaving only about 0.3% upside versus the prevailing trading level and signaling a more cautious stance on Muse's near-term revenue contribution.
The same article from Blockonomi noted that Evercore ISI reiterated an Outperform rating with a price objective of USD 860, JPMorgan upgraded Meta from Neutral to Overweight with a new target of USD 820, and KeyBanc kept an Overweight rating alongside a USD 780 target, all citing AI advances including Muse and the Meta Model application programming interface as key drivers.
Across the broader sell-side landscape, Blockonomi summarized that Meta currently enjoys a Strong Buy consensus built on 38 Buy ratings and 6 Hold ratings over the past three months, with an average price target of USD 759.43 that implies about 17% potential upside from recent levels.
These moves suggest that while some analysts question how quickly Muse will become a material profit driver, a critical mass of institutions still expects Meta's AI ecosystem to expand margins and cash flows over the medium term once the heavy investment phase moderates.
Stock performance and dividend signal investor confidence
Meta stock's recent trading and capital return plans add another layer to the story.
Per data from MarketBeat, Meta closed at USD 648.03 on Nasdaq on September 11, 2026, up 0.57% on the day, after trading in a session range between USD 646.20 and USD 664.24 and posting volume of about 16.9 million shares.
The same snapshot from MarketBeat indicates that at this price the shares sit 24.6% above the 52-week low of USD 520.26 but 18.1% below the 52-week high of USD 790.80, illustrating that the stock has already rallied strongly over the past year yet still trades at a discount to its recent peak.
According to StockAnalysis on September 13, 2026, Meta shares carry a trailing dividend yield of about 0.32% and trade at a price-to-earnings ratio of 24.41, which many investors view as a premium multiple but potentially justified by consensus forecasts for roughly 21.6% compound annual revenue growth over the next three years.
Recent options data compiled by Yahoo Finance show that Meta declared a cash dividend of USD 0.525 per share with an ex-dividend date of September 21, 2026, underlining the company's intent to combine heavy AI investment with direct cash returns to shareholders.
Next checkpoints for Meta Platforms stock
For Meta Platforms stock, the next key checkpoints will be whether Q3 2026 revenue lands inside the USD 61 billion to USD 64 billion guidance range and how quickly usage and monetization metrics for Muse and other AI agents scale from pilot users to broader adoption.
If management can show that the step-change in research and development spending seen in Q2 2026 is starting to translate into durable revenue and profit growth, while legal and regulatory costs normalize after the settlement around services for minors, the double-digit gap between the current share price and the mid-700s average target range offers tangible upside potential but also embeds execution risk.

Wells Fargo increased its Meta price target from $796 to $1,000 while maintaining an Overweight rating.
Analysts anticipate 2027 will mark a low point for earnings as AI infrastructure spending accelerates ahead of revenue generation in 2028.
Citi maintained its Buy rating, highlighting that Meta’s Muse assistant achieved 6.6 million downloads within 16 days as the leading app.
Meta shares increased 0.2% to reach $743.01, marking nearly 21% growth since Muse’s September 8 debut.
Central Pacific Bank Trust Division expanded its META holdings by 65% in the most recent quarter, valuing its position at approximately $5.2 million.
Shares of Meta Platforms edged up 0.2% to $743.01 during Tuesday’s session, extending the stock’s advance beyond 20% since early September. The gains follow a pair of analyst reports examining the social media giant’s artificial intelligence strategy.
Wells Fargo analyst Ken Gawrelski boosted his price objective to $1,000 from the previous $796 target. His Overweight recommendation remains unchanged.
However, the analyst’s outlook contains a cautionary element for the near term. Gawrelski anticipates that 2027 will represent a low point for Meta’s profitability.
The reasoning centers on Muse, Meta’s AI assistant, which isn’t expected to deliver significant revenue during that timeframe. At the same time, spending on infrastructure continues to escalate.
Gawrelski also flagged a $5 billion impact from discontinued capacity resales. Meta now requires that computing power for its proprietary AI offerings rather than leasing it to external parties.
His recommendation for shareholders: focus on the horizon beyond 2027. He projects 2028 as the inflection point when AI-driven revenue begins layering onto Meta’s core advertising operations.
An interesting detail emerged from the analysis. Gawrelski believes current Wall Street forecasts for 2027 remain overly bullish. He anticipates downward revisions as analysts absorb the delayed monetization timeline.
The Wells Fargo team drew parallels between the Muse deployment and Meta’s 2022 Reels transition. That strategic shift redirected user engagement from static posts to short-form video content, ultimately proving successful.
Citi analyst Ronald Josey delivered a more immediately optimistic assessment on Tuesday. He maintained his Buy rating alongside an $800 price objective.
Josey emphasized that Muse has surpassed 6.6 million downloads. The application has held the top position in download rankings for 16 consecutive days.
Citi’s long-term projection sees Muse generating more than $27 billion in revenue once fully scaled. Such figures represent meaningful contribution potential to Meta’s overall business.
Market reaction to both analyst notes proved muted. Share price movement remained minimal despite the positive commentary.
Institutional Investors Continue Accumulation
Beyond Wall Street research coverage, institutional capital continues flowing into the stock. Central Pacific Bank Trust Division increased its META holdings by 65% during the previous quarter.
The institution acquired an additional 2,817 shares, expanding its total position to 7,169 shares valued at roughly $5.2 million. Other smaller investment firms, including Watchman Group and Penney Financial, similarly expanded their allocations.
Nearly 80% of Meta’s outstanding shares are currently held by institutional investors and hedge funds. This represents substantial professional investment backing for the company.
According to MarketBeat data, the consensus analyst price target stands at $787.86. Individual targets span from a low of $700 to a high of $900.
Corporate insiders have not been accumulating shares recently. COO Javier Olivan and CEO Mark Zuckerberg both executed share sales in September through predetermined trading programs.
Total insider sales have reached approximately $99.9 million over the past 90 days. Company insiders maintain ownership of roughly 13.5% of outstanding shares.
Meta’s most recent quarterly results, released July 29, reported revenue of $60.80 billion. This exceeded analyst expectations of $60.22 billion and represented 28% growth compared to the prior year.
Earnings per share reached $6.18, falling short of the $7.19 consensus estimate. The company distributes a quarterly dividend of $0.525 per share, translating to approximately 0.3% yield.
Shares began Tuesday’s trading at $741.90, approaching the 12-month peak of $779.82.

White House Accord Draws Attention to Alphabet
Google CEO Sundar Pichai joined other major AI leaders in signing the accord at a White House lunch. The document outlines four layers of controls and audits for companies developing frontier models, including robust internal monitoring for cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats; an internal team to ensure controls function properly; partnership with an independent external auditor; and an independent board committee to oversee the process.
The agreement is voluntary and carries no formal enforcement mechanism, though Trump called it “morally binding.” Signatories also included Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, and xAI’s Elon Musk. The event underscored industry efforts at self-regulation amid ongoing debate over AI safety guardrails.

Apple stock posted a solid gain on the day. The company continues to expand its AI and services offerings while maintaining a large hardware and ecosystem business. Apple shares have responded to both product-cycle expectations and broader technology sentiment in recent sessions.
Meta Platforms stock edged lower despite Mark Zuckerberg’s participation in the White House signing. Meta Platforms remains a major player in AI development through its open-source and generative-AI efforts, alongside its core social and advertising platforms. The modest decline stood in contrast to the stronger moves in Alphabet and Apple shares.
The Invesco QQQ Trust’s advance indicated selective strength across large-cap technology. Traders also noted cloud concentration and the capital-market implications of heavy AI investment.
Similarities among Alphabet, Apple, and Meta Platforms include significant exposure to artificial intelligence and large-scale platform businesses. Differences appear in primary revenue drivers, with Alphabet leaning on search and cloud, Apple on hardware and services, and Meta Platforms on advertising and social engagement. The safety accord adds a policy dimension to the ongoing AI narrative.
The White House accord provides a framework for voluntary oversight but leaves room for further regulatory discussion. Alphabet’s AI infrastructure investments and cloud backlog remain key variables for investors tracking long-term returns on capital. Apple and Meta Platforms face their own execution and competitive dynamics within the AI and platform landscape.
Investors should consider keeping position sizes modest given the volatility that can accompany Big Tech and AI-related news flow. Meta Platforms (META -0.41%) has had an incredible September. At its peak, it rose more than 30%, although it sold off in the last few days of the month. Still, those are impressive results for Meta, especially given how poor its performance earlier in 2026 was.
It took that strong month for Meta to finally sit in positive year-to-date territory, but was this rally deserved? Let's take a look at what propelled it, and if those tailwinds are enough to maintain its momentum.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Meta's new product launch had the market buzzing
During September, Meta released a very important product: Muse -- a personal AI agent that can do all sorts of tasks for users. Muse can be tasked with multiple tasks and work in the background with user oversight before taking an action. This is the sort of thing the market has been waiting for Meta to release for a long time, and now that it's here, it's living up to expectations, judging by the market's reaction.

However, what investors will be curious about is how well Muse will do as an actual revenue source for the company. There have long been questions about how Meta will monetize its AI products, and as Muse is free to use, it doesn't address this problem.
However, there is a usage limit. If users find Muse a valuable enough tool that they want to make greater use of it than those limits allow, they'll need to upgrade to a paid subscription. Depending on how low Meta sets the usage limits and how useful the tool is, those subscriptions could become a massive new part of Meta's business, although it will be several quarters, at a minimum, before we can really gauge how it's being received and adopted.
Meta will likely make Muse a central talking point during its upcoming Q3 earnings report, which is expected in late October. After that, market sentiment may shift further regarding Meta stock. However, even after its major run-up, the stock isn't all that expensive.
META PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.
Entering September, Meta was trading at a pretty cheap 18 times forward earnings. Now, at 23 times forward earnings, it has reached a level most investors would expect a company of its caliber to trade at. However, it could still go higher, as it has in years past.
The market will need to know more about how Muse is adopted by consumers. If it continues to go well, it could help lift Meta's stock to new heights. If it doesn't, the market may send Meta back toward its recent valuation lows.

Those ads are deepfakes built with an AI copy of his face and voice, Cuban said, and Meta (NASDAQ:META) runs them anyway. "Facebook knows the little old ladies are getting ripped off," he said. He called the platform "the worst of the worst."
Cuban said some of the ads even include a disclaimer admitting the person on screen is AI-generated and the clip is meant as entertainment. By the time anyone gets to it, he argued, the pitch has already worked. "And to Facebook, that's good enough," he said.
"The point is, that defines the culture of the organization," Cuban said. A company that lets scammers go after people's grandparents, he argued, has shown what it will tolerate at every level.
Cuban does run a drug company — he co-founded Cost Plus Drugs, an online pharmacy that sells low-cost generic medications.
On Nov. 6, 2025, Reuters reported on internal Meta documents showing the company expected roughly $16 billion, or about 10% of its 2024 revenue, to flow in from ads pushing scams and prohibited products. By Meta's own internal count, users across its apps were seeing some 15 billion "higher risk" ads a day — the ones with obvious markers of fraud. One late 2024 document put that category's value at about $7 billion a year.
In a May 2025 presentation, Meta's own safety staff estimated the company's platforms play a part in a third of the scams that succeed in the U.S. Before Meta bans an advertiser, its automated systems must peg the account as at least 95% likely to be running a scam, the documents say. Below that threshold, the suspected scammer simply pays more per ad and stays live.
Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Reuters the documents "present a selective view that distorts Meta's approach to fraud and scams," and called the company's 10% estimate "rough and overly-inclusive." Complaints from users about scam ads had fallen 58% over the prior 18 months, he said at the time, and the company pulled down more than 134 million scam ads in 2025. The same documents note the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Meta over advertising tied to financial fraud.
Meanwhile, Meta's newest AI product has been causing headaches of its own. A Toronto man let the company's AI agent run his Facebook Marketplace listings on Sept. 26, and it gave a buyer his street address and said yes to a lowball offer. He later traced part of the problem to a permission setting he'd picked.

AI showed up in more than 3,100 of those complaints, and together those victims lost over $352 million. That's only counting the people who spoke up — plenty never file at all.
How to protect yourself — and your parents
Anytime you see a famous face advertising something pop up in your feed, assume it's fake — Cuban himself included in that. Run the product's name through a search with the word "scam" next to it. Then think about who in your family is on Facebook the most – and send them a message warning them about it.
And if you suspect anything fishy, file a report the same day to the Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov. The FBI froze $32.9 million worth of funds tied to older victims' cases in 2025, the agency says, but it can only chase money it knows about.

If you bought a popular tech sector ETF for broad technology exposure, open its most recent SEC portfolio filing. As of June 30, 2026, the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLK) held no shares of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Netflix, or Tesla. In the same filing, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction), Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) made up 35.87% of the fund. The ten largest positions came to 64.45%.
That gap between what’s missing and what dominates is the fund’s main limitation for investors seeking broad tech exposure. The word “technology” on the label covers a much narrower and more concentrated piece of the market than most buyers expect.
What Your Technology Fund Actually Holds
The filing lists 74 equity positions supporting about $123.9 billion in net assets. NVIDIA led at 14.65%, Apple came next at 12.85%, and Microsoft held 8.38%. Three more chip companies each had more than 5%, and chip equipment suppliers took up most of the other top-ten spots. At the other end, dozens of positions each made up less than 0.5% of assets.
So investors expecting broad exposure to the tech economy own a portfolio driven by a small group of semiconductor and hardware companies.
Why Alphabet and Amazon Fall Outside the Fund
XLK tracks a sector index built on the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS). GICS assigns every public company to exactly one sector. It puts Alphabet, Meta, and Netflix in Communication Services and Amazon and Tesla in Consumer Discretionary. XLK only holds companies classified as Information Technology.
GICS sorts companies by how they make money. Alphabet and Meta earn most of their revenue from advertising. Amazon’s classification follows its retail operations, and Tesla’s follows its vehicle manufacturing business. That means a highly technological business can still end up in a different sector.
All of this is disclosed and standard practice. The classification is public, and the fund follows its index. The cost comes from a common habit: few buyers read the sector definition before they buy a sector fund.
Concentration Risk Behind a Sector Label
When several of the biggest tech-adjacent companies are left out, the giants that remain carry more weight. With 74 stocks and 35.87% of assets in just three of them, XLK’s results depend heavily on NVIDIA, Apple, and Microsoft. A prolonged decline in any one of them could move the whole fund more than its name suggests.
That concentration has paid off recently. XLK gained 41.07% over the year ending October 5, 2026. Concentration amplifies losses as well as gains, and a retiree who draws income from a portfolio feels the losses more. Investors who want AI exposure without piling further into the same three chip and hardware names have options beyond the semiconductor sector (we covered seven of them, from power to cooling to networking, in a free report you can grab here).
XLK won’t give you either Alphabet or Amazon. Adding an S&P 500 fund changes the math in a way many investors miss. The broad fund already owns those companies at market weight, so XLK on top mostly adds more NVIDIA, Apple, and Microsoft to a portfolio that already holds them.
It works the other way too. If you already own large stakes in any of those three companies directly, buying XLK could double your exposure.
A Broader Tech ETF Includes Alphabet and Meta
The iShares U.S. Technology ETF (NYSEARCA:IYW) tracks the Russell 1000 Technology RIC 22.5/45 Capped Index, which classifies companies differently. Its top holdings have included Alphabet and Meta Platforms. The Vanguard Information Technology ETF follows a GICS-based index. It leaves out the same companies XLK does. Check each issuer’s current factsheet for expense ratios and top-ten weights before you compare.
XLK suits investors wanting concentrated exposure to the GICS Information Technology sector (chips, hardware, and enterprise software) and comfortable with a top-heavy portfolio. XLK is the wrong product for investors seeking broad technology exposure that includes the platforms most people call Big Tech.
Keep the dates in mind. These holdings come from the June 30, 2026 SEC filing. Weights change, and index providers review classifications from time to time, so a company can be moved to a different sector. Before you buy any sector fund, read the index methodology that defines the sector. That document tells you what you actually own.

The digital advertising landscape is shifting as artificial intelligence transforms how users find information and connect online. Choosing between Alphabet (GOOGL +0.35%) (GOOG +0.22%) and Meta Platforms (META -0.41%) requires weighing search dominance against social media scale.
Alphabet remains the primary gateway to the internet through its Google search engine and YouTube, while Meta dominates the social landscape with its massive family of apps. Both companies rely heavily on advertising revenue, but their paths to growth in artificial intelligence and the future of hardware are beginning to diverge significantly for investors of the communication sector.
Alphabet operates as a diversified technology holding company, primarily selling digital advertising space through its dominant Search platform and YouTube. It also provides cloud computing services to businesses and develops the Android operating system to support its mobile ecosystem.
In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $402.8 billion, representing a year-over-year growth of 15.1%. This expansion helped drive a net income of $132.2 billion, which was significantly higher than the profit recorded in the previous year. The net margin, which measures how much of each dollar in sales is kept as profit after all expenses, improved to 32.8% compared to the prior period.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.1x, indicating that total debt is very low relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at 2.0x, which means the company has twice as many short-term assets as short-term liabilities to cover its bills. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was $73.3 billion, which is the cash generated after paying for operations and capital expenditures.
Meta Platforms builds technologies for human connection through its family of apps, including Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. The company primarily generates revenue by selling highly targeted advertising space to marketers and creators who want to reach its billions of global users. It also offers consumer hardware products through its Reality Labs division, where it maintains complex relationships with mobile operating system providers such as Apple (AAPL +0.22%) and Google that influence its advertising effectiveness.
In FY 2025, revenue reached $201.0 billion, which indicates a robust growth rate of 22.2% from the prior year. Despite this revenue growth, net income was $60.5 billion, which was slightly lower than the profit recorded in the previous year. The net margin for the company was 30.1%, showing it remains highly profitable even as it spends on new initiatives, such as AI data centers.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.4x, suggesting a conservative amount of debt compared to its equity. The current ratio is 2.6x, providing a healthy cushion for the company to meet its immediate financial obligations with its existing assets. Free cash flow for the year was $46.1 billion.
Alphabet faces significant regulatory challenges, including a final judgment in a Department of Justice case that may require sharing search data or structural changes. The business is also sensitive to economic downturns that could reduce advertising spending across its Google search and YouTube platforms. Furthermore, the company must manage high capital costs for artificial intelligence infrastructure while facing competition from rivals such as Microsoft.
Meta recently settled a multistate lawsuit for $17.1 billion, which requires the company to implement sweeping child-safety reforms on its social platforms. It also faces ongoing risks from changes in mobile operating systems made by partners like Apple, which can limit the effectiveness of its advertising tools. Additionally, the Reality Labs segment continues to report persistent operating losses as the company tries to develop its long-term hardware and metaverse strategy.
While Meta Platforms offers higher top-line growth, Alphabet trades at a higher valuation multiple based on future earnings estimates and sales. Alphabet and Meta depend on digital advertising to support their businesses, yet both are looking to artificial intelligence to fuel success in future years. Alphabet is spending so much on building out its AI infrastructure, it reported negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion in the second quarter of 2026, as capital expenditures nearly doubled year over year to $44.9 billion.
Meta has fared better despite also nearly doubling capex, as its Q2 free cash flow totaled $784 million. However, that was a steep decline from 2025's free cash flow of $8.5 billion.
Yet that spending may be worth it. Meta's recent release of its Muse AI assistant achieved five million downloads in 22 days, more than popular AI tools such as ChatGPT. Even so, I would invest in Alphabet rather than Meta.
That's because Alphabet has so many ways in which it can employ AI to deliver business growth. Its Waymo autonomous ride-hailing business relies on AI as the driver for its vehicles. The company's cloud computing division, Google Cloud, through which it delivers its proprietary AI models to customers for a fee, experienced 82% year-over-year sales growth to $24.8 billion. This rapid rise in revenue indicates clients are adopting Alphabet's AI offerings, suggesting its capex spending can pay off in the long run.
